heading: Agents can retrieve check failures without you
expectation: The section claims that coding agents are able to fetch CI or check failures on their own, without a human passing the results to them.

heading: Let agents run checks and read failures
expectation: The section advises granting agents the ability to run project checks themselves and to read the resulting failure output.

heading: Stop relaying check failures by hand
expectation: The section claims that manually copying check failures to an agent is unnecessary work you should stop doing.

heading: The sponsor's performance claims remain unverified
expectation: The section cautions that the sponsor's claims about performance have not been verified, so the reader should not treat them as proven.

heading: Theo's chat test caught failures early
expectation: The section reports that an end-to-end chat test run by Theo caught failures at an early stage.

heading: Test that the other person receives it
expectation: The section advises testing that a message or action sent by one side is actually received by the other side, rather than only testing the sending side.

heading: Separate checks can miss broken interactions
expectation: The section claims that testing each component in isolation can fail to detect bugs that appear only in the interaction between them.

heading: The recalled test has no implementation here
expectation: The section clarifies that the test Theo recalled in the story does not exist in this handbook's accompanying code or examples.

heading: Shared automation can speed up every agent
expectation: The section claims that automation shared across the team benefits all agents working concurrently, speeding each of them up.

heading: Fix shared delays before adding more agents
expectation: The section advises removing shared bottlenecks or delays before scaling up the number of concurrent agents.

heading: Concurrent agents benefit from removing shared delays
expectation: The section claims that when several agents run at once, eliminating a shared delay improves throughput for all of them.

heading: The automation gains have not been measured
expectation: The section cautions that the claimed speedups from the automation have not actually been measured.

heading: Remote agent work makes previews more valuable
expectation: The section claims that when agents work remotely rather than locally, preview environments become more valuable to the workflow.

heading: Give agents previews they can reach and test
expectation: The section advises providing preview environments that agents can access and verify on their own.

heading: Previews help when local review is impractical
expectation: The section claims preview environments are most useful when reviewing changes locally is not practical.

heading: Deployment needs separate authorization
expectation: The section notes that deploying preview environments is an externally-visible action requiring separate authorization, which is out of scope here.
alternate: The section claims that in real deployments, creating preview environments requires a separate approval step from the development work itself.

heading: Theo built a tool for agent uploads
expectation: The section reports that Theo built a custom tool so agents could upload files.

heading: Confirm existing tools cannot upload before building
expectation: The section advises verifying that no existing tool can already perform the upload before investing in a custom one.

heading: Build upload tools only for recurring gaps
expectation: The section claims custom upload tooling is justified only when the gap recurs, not for one-off needs.

heading: Upload instructions do not prove successful uploads
expectation: The section cautions that giving an agent instructions for uploading does not demonstrate the upload actually succeeded.

heading: Theo finds small agent tools rewarding
expectation: The section reports that Theo personally finds writing small tools for agents satisfying or worthwhile.

heading: Replace one recurring workaround with a small tool
expectation: The section suggests picking one workaround you repeat often and replacing it with a small purpose-built tool.

heading: Try small tools when bigger efforts discourage you
expectation: The section claims small tool projects are a good entry point when larger automation efforts feel daunting or demotivating.

heading: Theo's enjoyment does not establish productivity gains
expectation: The section cautions that Theo finding the work enjoyable is not evidence that such tools improve productivity.

heading: Theo sees more support for tooling work
expectation: The section reports that Theo observes growing team support for spending time on tooling work.

heading: Ask for limited time to improve shared tools
expectation: The section advises requesting a bounded amount of time, rather than open-ended commitment, to work on shared tools.

heading: Recheck assumptions that managers oppose tooling work
expectation: The section claims you should question the assumption that management will reject tooling work, since support may be greater than expected.

heading: Does your team welcome time spent on tools?
expectation: The section poses a reflective question asking whether your own team would support time spent on tooling, implying the answer varies.

heading: Repeated failures waste tokens
expectation: The section claims that when agents keep failing on the same class of mistake, the retry loop consumes tokens wastefully.

heading: Make the corrections automatic
expectation: The section advises turning corrections for recurring mistakes into automated checks or fixes rather than repeating them manually.

heading: Automate corrections that keep returning in reviews
expectation: The section claims review comments that recur across changes are good candidates for automation.

heading: Overly broad checks can reject good changes
expectation: The section cautions that automated checks written too broadly may reject legitimate changes.

heading: Cheaper rule writing can make checks worthwhile
expectation: The section claims that agents make writing custom lint rules cheap enough that checks previously not worth the cost become worthwhile.

heading: Reassess the cost of rejected check ideas
expectation: The section advises revisiting check ideas you previously rejected as too expensive, since the cost calculation has changed.

heading: Revisit manual checks once automation becomes affordable
expectation: The section claims manual checks should be revisited for automation when the cost of automating them drops.

heading: Custom checks still need maintenance and review
expectation: The section cautions that custom checks carry ongoing maintenance and review costs even when cheap to create.

heading: Unwritten project knowledge holds newcomers back
expectation: The section claims that project knowledge existing only in people's heads slows down newcomers, including new agents.

heading: Record recurring corrections for everyone's agents
expectation: The section advises writing down corrections you make repeatedly so all agents and teammates benefit.

heading: Write down project rules you keep explaining
expectation: The section claims rules you find yourself explaining repeatedly should be written down once for everyone.

heading: Theo disputes equal effectiveness without engineering experience
expectation: The section reports Theo's disagreement with a claim that documentation or tooling makes agents equally effective regardless of engineering experience.
alternate: The section quotes Theo disputing that a non-engineer, given the same written knowledge, would work as effectively as an experienced engineer.

heading: Newcomer questions reveal unclear project guidance
expectation: The section claims that questions from newcomers, human or agent, signal gaps or ambiguity in the project's written guidance.

heading: Answer newcomer questions and fix their causes
expectation: The section advises both answering newcomer questions and updating the underlying guidance so the question does not recur.

heading: Repeated confusion points to missing project guidance
expectation: The section claims that the same confusion arising repeatedly indicates documentation or guidance is missing.

heading: Make questions safe without requiring daily quotas
expectation: The section cautions that encouraging questions should not take the form of mandatory question quotas; safety to ask matters more than volume.

heading: Theo recommends writing agent instructions yourself
expectation: The section reports Theo's recommendation that you author your agent instructions yourself rather than accepting generated ones unedited.

heading: Revise instructions yourself after observing agent behavior
expectation: The section advises personally editing your instruction files based on what you observe the agent actually doing.

heading: Revisit generated instructions you have never revised
expectation: The section suggests auditing instruction files that were generated once and never personally reviewed or edited.

heading: Theo's writing preference does not override your instructions
expectation: The section clarifies that Theo's stated preference is advice, not a rule that overrides your own project's instructions or judgment.

heading: Written rules can guide agents to refuse requests
expectation: The section claims that written project rules can cause agents to push back on or refuse requests that violate those rules.

heading: Write down recurring refusals and their reasons
expectation: The section advises documenting the requests you routinely decline, along with the reasons, in your project instructions.

heading: Explain project boundaries when unwanted requests recur
expectation: The section claims that when agents repeatedly make unwanted requests, stating the project boundary in writing resolves it.

heading: Written refusal rules can be bypassed
expectation: The section cautions that written refusal rules are not guaranteed enforcement and can be circumvented.

heading: Connected data rules can check whole application paths
expectation: The section claims that when data definitions are connected through the type system, checks can validate entire paths through the application rather than isolated pieces.

heading: Reuse data definitions instead of copying them
expectation: The section advises sharing a single data definition across layers instead of duplicating it in multiple places.

heading: Connect duplicated data definitions when they drift apart
expectation: The section claims that duplicated definitions that have diverged should be connected or unified, since drift causes bugs.

heading: You need not adopt Theo's chosen technologies
expectation: The section clarifies that the principle matters more than the specific technologies Theo used, which you are free to skip.

heading: Written project knowledge reduces repeated explanations to agents
expectation: The section claims that documenting project knowledge eliminates the need to re-explain the same things to agents each session.

heading: Test whether project files explain enough to newcomers
expectation: The section advises verifying your project files by checking whether a newcomer, with no other context, can work from them alone.

heading: First tasks reveal explanations missing from project files
expectation: The section claims that a newcomer's first tasks are the best way to discover what the project files fail to explain.

heading: Better documentation does not guarantee equal newcomer performance
expectation: The section cautions that improving documentation does not ensure newcomers will perform as well as experienced members.

heading: Try default tools before adding more
expectation: The section claims that the default setup should be tried first before adding extra tools or context.

heading: Add only what observed agent failures show missing
expectation: The section advises adding tools or context only when an observed agent failure demonstrates the gap.

heading: Test new setups before installing extra tools
expectation: The section claims a fresh setup should be tested as-is before assuming extra tools are needed.

heading: Testing defaults does not restrict authorized tool authoring
expectation: The section clarifies that recommending a test-first approach does not forbid writing your own tools where authorized.

heading: File locations alone cannot guide good decisions
expectation: The section claims that listing file locations does not help an agent make good decisions; decision guidance is what matters.

heading: Write decision guidance beyond listing file locations
expectation: The section advises writing instructions that explain how to decide, not just where things live.

heading: Revise instructions dominated by directory lists
expectation: The section suggests rewriting instruction files that consist mostly of directory listings.

heading: Brief file location guidance can still help
expectation: The section concedes that short file-location references still have some value, qualifying the main claim.

heading: Improving others' contributions may help your career
expectation: The section claims that work improving other people's output, such as shared tooling, can advance your own career.

heading: Make shared contributions visible
expectation: The section advises ensuring your shared-improvement work is visible to those who evaluate you.

heading: Consider team improvements when recognizing senior work
expectation: The section claims that evaluating senior engineers should include the improvements they made for the whole team, not just their individual output.

heading: Employers may not reward shared tooling work
expectation: The section cautions that employers do not necessarily reward shared tooling work, qualifying the career-leverage claim.

heading: Theo's solo projects outgrew his own understanding
expectation: The section reports that Theo's solo-built projects grew beyond what he could hold in his own head.

heading: Document solo projects for someone new to contribute
expectation: The section advises documenting your solo project as if a newcomer were about to contribute to it.

heading: Add guidance when solo code outpaces your memory
expectation: The section claims that once your solo codebase exceeds what you remember, written guidance becomes necessary.

heading: Your solo project may still fit your memory
expectation: The section qualifies the advice by noting that a small enough solo project may not yet need this documentation.
